Sound, in its physical definition, consists of longitudinal pressure waves propagating through a medium. Musical pitch corresponds to wave frequency (measured in hertz), while loudness correlates with amplitude (measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale). Timbre, the quality that distinguishes a clarinet from a trumpet playing the same note, results from the specific distribution of harmonic overtones.

Western tonal music is organized around the twelve-tone equal temperament system, in which the octave is divided into twelve semitones of equal frequency ratio (specifically, the twelfth root of two, approximately 1.05946). This represents a mathematical compromise; pure intervals (those derived from simple frequency ratios) cannot all be accommodated simultaneously within a fixed tuning system. The resulting slight deviations from pure intonation are generally imperceptible to untrained listeners.

Rhythm introduces a temporal dimension. Time signatures (such as 4/4 or 3/4) establish a metrical framework, but skilled performers routinely deviate from strict metronomic timing through techniques collectively termed "expressive timing" or rubato. These micro-deviations, paradoxically, enhance rather than diminish the perception of musical coherence.
